title: No Favorites at God's Judgment
overview: Paul argues that everyone, Jewish or not, will be judged fairly by how they actually live, so no one is safe simply by condemning others or by having religious privileges.

parts.label: Judging others (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Paul turns to anyone who nodded along with the list of wrongs at the end of chapter 1, pointing out that they do the same things they condemn. Treating God's patience as permission misses its point, which is to lead a person to a change of heart.

parts.label: Judged by what we do (vv. 5-11)
parts.note: A stubborn heart is pictured as saving up anger like hoarded treasure, to be released on a coming day of judgment. God repays each person by their actions, the Jewish people first and then everyone else, because God plays no favorites.

parts.label: A law written on hearts (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: People who never had the law given through Moses are not judged by it, yet when they do what it asks, it shows its sense is written inside them, with conscience arguing for and against them. Paul says God will judge even hidden things through Jesus.

parts.label: Teaching others, not oneself (vv. 17-24)
parts.note: Paul, himself Jewish, speaks to an imagined fellow Jew who sees the law as making him a guide for others, and asks whether he keeps it himself. Scholars are unsure whether robbing temples means stealing from pagan shrines or disrespecting holy things more broadly, and the closing quotation comes from Isaiah 52:5.

parts.label: Circumcision of the heart (vv. 25-29)
parts.note: Circumcision was the physical sign marking Jewish men as part of God's covenant, a binding agreement with Abraham's family. Paul says the outward sign means little without an inner change, an idea the Hebrew Bible itself voices when it calls for hearts to be circumcised (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4).

disagreement: Christians differ over who the people are who actually keep the law and are counted right with God (vv. 13, 26-27): some read this as a hypothetical no one meets, setting up chapter 3, while others see real people, such as Christians changed by God's Spirit or non-Jews who follow their conscience.
think: Why do you think it is often easier to spot a fault in someone else than to notice the same fault in yourself?
